speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House a matter that would have a devastating impact upon intercollegiate sports in both western Canada and the Atlantic region. The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) has decided to reallocate substantially the travel subsidy that is used to support athletic teams in both western Canada and the Atlantic region to move from university to university. The Minister made that decision without any prior consultation at all with the CIAU or the universities involved. They have sent him numerous telegrams asking for a meeting. If they do not have a meeting by June 27 intercollegiate sports in the Atlantic region and western Canada could come to an end.
This morning I call on all the Members of this House to make every effort to have the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport meet with the CIU and come to grips with this very important issue before we Find collegiate sports are destroyed in Canada; and that Minister will be held responsible.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING NEW REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one month ago the Minister for Immigration (Mr. McLean) announced a program for reducing the backlog of refugee claimants in Canada.
Unfortunately it seems that he did not follow through with action. According to immigration lawyers in Toronto the regulations that were to be gazetted this week so refugee claimants, their lawyers, and immigration officers could know what they are doing, have still not been gazetted and will not be gazetted until next month or later. There is dreadful confusion. No new staff has even been hired, as promised, so that the existing staff is hopelessly overloaded. No new office has been opened, as promised.
The Refugee Status Advisory Committee, having made space in its calendar, is receiving no fast-track cases.
Clearly, false refugee claimants are coming in literally by the plane load, at nearly 1,000 per month, and the Minister has done nothing to stop this. What is the Minister doing to carry out the program he promised?

subsubtopic: RESULTS OF SUBTERRANEAN AGRICULTURAL EXPERIMENTS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, subterranean agriculture may well become a growth industry in western Canada. Experiments in worked-out areas of the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan mines appear to be showing positive results.
The advantages of such underground culture include a steady 80 temperature, no snow, hail, tempest or other natural occurrence which could damage crops, and an environment which is free of insects and other pests.
Light, fertilizer, and a growing medium must, of course, be provided. Cucumbers are said to thrive, and good results are being obtained with other vegetables, seedlings, and flowers.
Such innovations which, if successful, could add significantly to Canada's range of agricultural products, are certainly to be applauded.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN UKRAINIAN VETERANS' REUNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Canadian Ukrainian veterans of the wars held their reunion and meetings last week, it was the first of its kind in Canada. Delegates, men and women of Ukrainian origin from across the country and even the United States and England, arrived in Edmonton to discuss mutual concerns and assistance for those in need. Naturally, old acquaintances were renewed, many for the first time in over 40 years. Also present were two veterans of World War I.

June 20, 1986
One of the highlights was the sod-turning ceremony at the Ukrainian Heritage Village, 35 miles east of Edmonton, where a statue of Michael Luchkowich, the first Member of Parliament of Ukrainian racial origin, will be erected. Another highlight was the official opening of the veterans' section in the Ukrainian Museum and Archives documenting the many contributions made by the Ukrainian veterans during the wars.
Ukrainian Canadians served with courage and pride, defending freedom for Canada. We pay tribute to them.

subsubtopic: ELIGIBILITY REGULATION CHANGE-EFFECT ON SEASONAL WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over
10.000	farmworkers in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, as well as other seasonal workers such as loggers and fishers, have recently been dealt a very serious blow by the Conservative Government. subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT PERFORMANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the latest economic indicators point to sustained economic growth in Quebec. Since the advent of this Government, 160,000 new jobs have been created in Quebec. The unemployment rate now stands at 10.6 per cent, the first time in five years when it is under 11 per cent.
The value of building permits in the first quarter of this year rose by 54 per cent. Additional investments in the building sector in 1985 topped $833 million. Building starts in May 1986 were 69 per cent higher that in the same month last year.
June 20, 1986

Farm bankruptcies in Quebec have gone down 50 per cent since 1984.
And 33.2 per cent of small businesses in Quebec had additional capital investment projects in the first six months of 1986.
These positive results flow from our economic renewal policy.

subsubtopic: MONTREAL ECONOMIC SUMMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1986 Montreal Economic Summit came to a close yesterday. During this Summit, business participants expressed their views and reached a consensus on many issues.
The representatives of those involved proposed resolutions which were adopted unanimously on matters such as the establishment of business zones, recognition by the Federal Government of Montreal as the Canadian centre of the aerospace industry; the creation of a high technology education centre; and the use of incubators, to name but a few.
Mr. Speaker, if we recall the interventions of the federal Conservative Ministers, we find that they have also made commitments on these same matters. It follows that the Conservative Government is aware of the concerns of the people of Montreal, that it knows the aspirations of the business participants and that it takes action to help them.

Mr. Speaker, "yesterday evening, before the Ottawa Carleton Board of Trade, the Liberal Leader remained silent about the position of his party on the development of trade between Canada and the United States." This is what Manon Cornellier said this morning in the newspaper La Presse.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party must really be weakened if it is unable to take a position on negotiations with our major trading partner. We export for $95 billion a year to the United States, which accounts for 80 per cent of all our exports.
Mr. Speaker, when the Liberal Leader can only talk gibberish about the negotiations, it shows incompetence. When his associates go around in circles, it shows gross complacency. When the Liberals put their thirst for power before the development of trade, it is a betrayal. In this area as in all others, the Liberals are disciples of Janus.

subsubtopic: AUSTRIAN PRESIDENT-ELECT-CALL FOR INVESTIGATION OF WARTIME ACTIVITY ALLEGATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, immediately after the election of Mr. Kurt Waldheim as President of Austria I made a statement in the House calling upon the Canadian Government to direct its United Nations Ambassador to press for a thorough, independent, international investigation of the serious wartime allegations which have been made about Mr. Waldheim.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN POSITION ON IMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC SANCTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. The situation in South Africa continues to deteriorate daily, and Canadians have now seen the House of Representatives unanimously support the imposition of severe economic sanctions. Canadians are wondering why it is necessary to delay further a leadership role for Canada and the imposition of effective economic sanctions at this time.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN POSITION ON IMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC SANCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to hear my hon. friend say that there is a denial of a leadership role for Canada. We tried to play the traditional Canadian role played by my predecessors in other circumstances when we were in Nassau.
In this case there are two important considerations. Of course the dismantling of apartheid in South Africa, a grave and growing evil, is the objective of all Hon. Members of the House. How we do it as members of the Commonwealth is also an important strategic consideration. We may be wrong, but it is our judgment that we can best accomplish this quite noble objective by making sure that the Commonwealth stays together and that there is unity of purpose and action. That requires the measured, reasonable course of action that we have been following and on which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has set out.
I will be meeting with Mrs. Thatcher on the 13th followed by a meeting of the seven Heads of Government of Commonwealth countries in London the first week of August. It is our hope that we can contribute substantially toward advancing in

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of Transport
subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CRASH OF AIR-IND1A FLIGHT 182
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to remind the House, and all Canadians, of a tragic yet important anniversary in the aviation world.
On Sunday, June 23, 1985, Air-India Flight 182, enroute to England from Toronto and Montreal crashed into the North Atlantic off Ireland killing all 329 persons onboard.
On this anniversary of the Air-India disaster all Members of this House, and indeed all Canadians, feel again the deep sorrow and sadness at such a tragic loss of life.
The observation of the anniversary involves three countries, Canada, India and Ireland. On June 23, 1986 Canada will be participating in the benediction of a special memorial erected on land donated to Canada and India in perpetuity by the Government of Ireland on the seaside of Dunmanus Bay 200 miles west of where Flight 182 plunged into the grey Atlantic a year ago. The memorial bears this simple inscription, "In honour of those who died in the Air India flight".
At this time I want to extend once more our thanks and appreciation to the Government and citizens of Ireland for their tireless efforts in assisting with the search and the compassion and concern which they showed to the relatives and friends of the deceased while at Cork.
The Air-India tragedy, the bombing of Canadian Pacific Air Flight 003 at Narita Airport in Japan, and subsequent international terrorist attacks against civil aviation have generated a need for improved airport and aviation security throughout the world. For our part we have responded to this new reality and have continued to upgrade and improve our security procedures and equipment. Our desire is sincere and our efforts are unceasing to ensure that Canadians do not suffer from international terrorism in the future.
As we once again turn our minds to Cork and the Atlantic where the victims of the Air-India disaster perished we think of the sadness and sense of loss endured by the relatives and the friends of those victims. We pledge to them, to this House, and to all Canadians our Government's continued commitment and

June 20, 1986
Committee Reports
dedicated efforts to ensure the safety and security of our air transportation system.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CRASH OF AIR-IND1A FLIGHT 182
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party of Canada, and on behalf of all my Liberal colleagues in the House of Commons, I want to express again to the families of the victims our deep sorrow and sadness for the tragic loss of these 329 lives.
I must comment at this time on the regretful decision by the Government to reject a plea for help from 70 grieving Canadians who want to make an ocean ferry pilgrimage to the crash site of the Air-India Flight 182, and perform last rites for family victims in accordance with their religious beliefs. I think it is regrettable that the Government was not able to find the $60,000 necessary for such a trip. It has just been confirmed by the Government, but they still have the weekend to think it over.
I think the Government should indeed reflect during the weekend, and make this money available. After all, as the organizer of this pilgrimage said, it is not a very large amount very big thing considering the magnitude of the tragedy and the fact that they are Canadians from coast to coast who have this compelling and emotional need.
I appreciate the efforts of the Government to try to improve security at our airports. I will have other occasions to say that 1 am not too happy with what the Government is doing. 1 have long felt that security at airports should become the total responsibility of the Government instead of being the responsibility of private companies who are submitting bids and are trying to make money out of the performance of this duty. I think because of worldwide terrorism it would be justifiable now for the Department of Transport to take over this responsibility and pay for it.
In closing, I want to say that this tragic incident, which so terribly affected so many Canadian families, should not be repeated. Our sorrow and our thoughts on Monday will be with these families of the victims. Indeed, I hope that in the few hours that are left, the Government will come back with a favourable decision. It is tourist season and the cost for many of these families to go to Europe is heavy. The Government should make the appropriate accommodations for them in Ireland to respect their religious way of paying respect to their families.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CRASH OF AIR-IND1A FLIGHT 182
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CRASH OF AIR-IND1A FLIGHT 182
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues, I join with the Minister and the Official Opposition in renewing our heartfelt sympathies and regrets. We send our best wishes to the friends and families of those who died in the Air-India disaster one year ago.
I know all of us in the House and all Canadians well remember the day of the crash and how we shared in Canada and with people around the world, particularly in India, the
horror and shock of the magnitude of the tragedy. Our memories about this will be long, as they should be. Hopefully we will learn and profit from our memories of those who died.
I want to add our gratitude to the Government and the people of Ireland for their great efforts and their gesture. It is something that should happen more often in the international scene.
The Minister knows that he will be supported by Members on this side of the House with any intiatives he undertakes to minimize the risk of air travel and the risk at airports. We also continue to push, as we have for a number of years, to have Transport Canada and the RCMP entirely responsible for airport security instead of the airlines themselves. However, the debate of how best to achieve those results will continue at another time.
I hope the Minister and Canada will provide even more leadership in the international scene, with international agencies in other countries, to strengthen airport and airline security in many more nations. There are still too many nations where that security is not very good.
Let us remember the incident and the great responsibility that has been thrust on all of us to do more in the hope that this will never happen again. As we do so, let us also remember that we hold the key to minimizing the grief of those who lost loved ones by ever being on guard against those few who would use this tragedy or any similar tragedy to broadly label cultural and religious groups. Many innocent people died in that Air-India flight. Let us also treat fairly in our hearts and minds the innocent who live among us here today. Again, our best wishes for a better future for the friends and families of the victims of the Air Indian disaster.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: LACK OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION AT COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to the House that on June 17 a meeting of the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry had to be postponed because there were no interpreters.

subsubtopic: LACK OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION AT COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext:
The Chair and the House are aware of that matter. I indicated earlier, in response to a similar comment about another committee by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), that part of the problem is that we now have so many committees that there are more committees than the Secretary of State can provide translation for. Translation is provided to the committees and the House, not by the House itself, but by the Secretary of State.
That matter is currently under discussion with the Department in order to try to resolve these matters.

subsubtopic: LACK OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION AT COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe that when we began the legislative committee process there was an understanding among Members of the House that we would attempt to have the legislative committees meet when the House was sitting, while the standing committees and other committees would meet when the House was not sitting. I note that many standing committees are not doing that and I think this is putting some pressure on the Translation and contributing to the problem. I wanted to make certain that we all understood that that may be contributing to the problem.

subsubtopic: LACK OF SIMULTANEOUS TRANSLATION AT COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member.
